vent from the overall message carried by a train of such events."},{"question":"Can you explain: Why myelin makes a difference?","answer":"Myelin insulates portions of many axons. The membrane is exposed at nodes of Ranvier, so action potentials are renewed at spaced intervals, a pattern called saltatory conduction. This makes long-distance signaling faster and more energy-efficient than repeatedly regenerating the signal over every small membrane segment. Not every neuron uses myelinated long axons: local neurons can process information over short distances with graded changes in membrane voltage. Distinguish such local potentials from the all-or-none signals of axons."}],"deepContentStart":10,"deepTopics":[{"id":"bp14-m1-3-h01","title":"The Resting Potential of the membrane.","printedPage":26,"pdfPage":44,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":18},{"text":"However, the membrane is selectively permeable , letting some in.","printedPage":26,"pdfPage":44,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":21},{"text":"Because of this pump, sodium ions are more than 10 times more concentrated outside the membrane than inside, and potassium ions are more concentrated inside than outside.","printedPage":26,"pdfPage":44,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":22},{"text":"The sodium–potassium pump is effective only because the selective permeability of the membrane prevents the sodium ions that were pumped out from leaking back in to push sodium into the cell.","printedPage":27,"pdfPage":45,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":25},{"text":"Sodium is positively charged, and the proteins.","printedPage":27,"pdfPage":45,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":26},{"text":"The other force is the concentration gradient , the difference provided:","printedPage":28,"pdfPage":46,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":39},{"text":"Any subthreshold stimulation produces a small response that depolarization that reaches or passes the threshold produces an action potential.","printedPage":28,"pdfPage":46,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":44},{"text":"For a given neuron, all action potentials are approximately equal in amplitude","printedPage":28,"pdfPage":46,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":45},{"text":"Slight variations occur spontaneously, but not because of the stimulus.","printedPage":29,"pdfPage":47,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":46},{"text":"More properly stated, the all-or-none law is that the amplitude and velocity of an action potential are independent of the intensity of the stimulus that initiated it, provided that the stimulus reaches the threshold.","printedPage":29,"pdfPage":47,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":47},{"text":"By analogy, imagine flushing a toilet: You need to press at least a certain strength (the threshold), but pressing harder does not make the toilet flush faster or more vigorously.","printedPage":29,"pdfPage":47,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":48},{"text":"The all-or-none law constrains how an axon can send a message.","printedPage":29,"pdfPage":47,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":49},{"text":"To signal the difference between a weak stimulus and a strong stimulus, all that an axon can change is the frequency of its action potentials, or their timing.","printedPage":29,"pdfPage":47,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":50},{"text":"For example, a taste axon shows one rhythm of responses for sweet tastes and a different rhythm for bitter tastes .","printedPage":29,"pdfPage":47,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":51}],"sourceWordCount":251},{"id":"bp14-m1-3-h06","title":"The Molecular Basis of channel.","printedPage":29,"pdfPage":47,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":53},{"text":"At first, opening the potassium channels makes little neuron.","printedPage":29,"pdfPage":47,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":54},{"text":"Of all the sodium ions near the axon, less than 1 percent cross the membrane during an action potential, and sodium ions remain far more concentrated outside than inside.","printedPage":29,"pdfPage":47,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":55},{"text":"Because of the concentration gradient, sodium ions would continue to enter the cell, except that the sodium gates snap shut at the peak of the action potential.","printedPage":29,"pdfPage":47,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":56},{"text":"Because the potassium channels remain open after the sodium channels close, enough potassium leaves to drive the membrane back to its original level and then slightly beyond it.","printedPage":29,"pdfPage":47,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":57},{"text":"At the end of this process, the membrane has returned to its resting potential, but the inside of the neuron has slightly more sodium ions and slightly fewer potassium ions than before.","printedPage":29,"pdfPage":47,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":58},{"text":"However, excessive stimulation occurs only under abnormal conditions, such as during a stroke or after the use of certain drugs.","printedPage":29,"pdfPage":47,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":59}],"sourceWordCount":504},{"id":"bp14-m1-3-h07","title":"Propagation of the offspring.","printedPage":30,"pdfPage":48,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":62},{"text":"In a sense, the action potential gives birth to a new action axon and propagates without loss from start to finish.","printedPage":30,"pdfPage":48,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":64},{"text":"The cell body and dendrites do not conduct action potentials, but they passively register the electrical event that started in the nearby axon.","printedPage":30,"pdfPage":48,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":65},{"text":"This back-propagation is important: When an action potential back-propagates into a dendrite, the dendrite becomes more susceptible to the structural changes responsible for learning.","printedPage":30,"pdfPage":48,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":66},{"text":"Everything follows logically from the facts that voltage-gated millisecond.","printedPage":31,"pdfPage":49,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":70},{"text":"This period is the absolute refractory period , the time it.","printedPage":29,"pdfPage":47,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":57},{"text":"At the end of this process, the membrane has returned to its resting typically negative relative to the outside. This stored gradient is the starting condition for signaling.","paragraphIndex":20000,"bullets":[{"label":"Typical value","explanation":"A frequently used approximate resting potential is −70 millivolts, though the precise value depends on cell type and conditions. Voltage always compares two locations.","paragraphIndex":20001},{"label":"Measurement","explanation":"An electrode inside the axon and another outside reveal the difference; the number does not mean that the whole cell has a uniform negative charge everywhere.","paragraphIndex":20002},{"label":"How it is measured","explanation":"Electrodes inside and outside the cell detect a difference in electrical charge.","paragraphIndex":52300},{"label":"What maintains it","explanation":"Selective membrane permeability and active ion transport maintain unequal ion distributions. Changes in this balance alter the probability of generating an action potential.","paragraphIndex":52301}],"status":"original_classroom_note_sample","basis":"provided_book_pdf_and_markdown","followUpExplanation":"A resting neuron maintains an electrical potential across its membrane, with the interior generally more negative than the exterior. This voltage is a prepared state, not an absence of biological activity.","followUpParagraphIndex":52100,"depth":"comprehensive_masters_with_expanded_explanations","studyDepth":"standard_existing"},{"headingId":"bp14-m1-3-h02","title":"Forces Acting on Sodium and Potassium Ions","level":2,"parentId":"bp14-m1-3-h01","printedPage":26,"pdfPage":44,"explanation":"The resting voltage reflects both concentration differences and electrical attraction or repulsion acting on ions. Membrane permeability determines which force can produce movement at a given time.","paragraphIndex":20003,"bullets":[{"label":"Sodium and potassium","explanation":"Sodium is more concentrated outside; potassium is more concentrated inside. Concentration gradients favor diffusion toward the less concentrated side.","paragraphIndex":20004},{"label":"Pump and leakage","explanation":"The sodium–potassium pump uses energy to export three sodium ions for every two potassium ions it imports, while selective potassium permeability contributes to the negative resting voltage.","paragraphIndex":20005},{"label":"Concentration gradient","explanation":"An ion tends to move from regions where it is more abundant toward regions where it is less abundant, when channels allow it.","paragraphIndex":52302},{"label":"Electrical gradient","explanation":"Charged particles also respond to voltage. A membrane can therefore favor one direction of movement chemically and another electrically, producing an equilibrium potential.","paragraphIndex":52303}],"status":"original_classroom_note_sample","basis":"provided_book_pdf_and_markdown","followUpExplanation":"The movement of sodium and potassium reflects two distinct forces: electrical attraction and differences in concentration. Both must be considered when predicting the direction of ion movement.","followUpParagraphIndex":52101,"depth":"comprehensive_masters_with_expanded_explanations","studyDepth":"detailed_existing"},{"headingId":"bp14-m1-3-h03","title":"Why a Resting Potential?","level":2,"parentId":"bp14-m1-3-h01","printedPage":28,"pdfPage":46,"explanation":"The cell spends energy to maintain an electrical readiness state. The resting potential is useful precisely because a stimulus can quickly change membrane permeability and release this stored potential for signaling.","paragraphIndex":20006,"bullets":[{"label":"Readiness","explanation":"Maintained sodium gradients let sodium rush inward when appropriate voltage-gated channels open.","paragraphIndex":20007},{"label":"Cost and benefit","explanation":"Pumps consume energy continuously, but prepare the neuron to transmit a rapid message without needing to create a new chemical gradient first.","paragraphIndex":20008},{"label":"Stored readiness","explanation":"An established gradient lets opening a channel rapidly change membrane voltage without first building a new concentration difference.","paragraphIndex":52304},{"label":"Energy cost","explanation":"Ion pumps help maintain long-term sodium and potassium gradients; they do not produce each action potential by directly pumping its rapid voltage rise.","paragraphIndex":52305}],"status":"original_classroom_note_sample","basis":"provided_book_pdf_and_markdown","followUpExplanation":"Maintaining the resting potential requires energy, but the result allows the neuron to respond quickly when stimulated. The separation of charge is a functional preparation for communication.","followUpParagraphIndex":52102,"depth":"comprehensive_masters_with_expanded_explanations","studyDepth":"concise_existing"},{"headingId":"bp14-m1-3-h04","title":"The Action Potential","level":1,"parentId":null,"printedPage":28,"pdfPage":46,"explanation":"An action potential is a rapid, stereotyped reversal and recovery of membrane voltage that occurs when depolarization reaches threshold. It differs from a small local change that fades without triggering a spike.","paragraphIndex":20009,"bullets":[{"label":"Before threshold","explanation":"Weak depolarization shifts the voltage toward zero but usually subsides. Hyperpolarization moves the voltage farther from the firing threshold.","paragraphIndex":20010},{"label":"At threshold","explanation":"Voltage-gated channels open in a regenerative sequence, producing a full spike that can travel along the axon.","paragraphIndex":20011},{"label":"Threshold and triggering","explanation":"Sufficient depolarization opens voltage-dependent channels and initiates a rapid response. Hyperpolarization generally moves the membrane farther from threshold.","paragraphIndex":52306},{"label":"Sequence","explanation":"A rapid depolarizing phase is followed by repolarization and a period in which another spike is difficult or impossible to initiate.","paragraphIndex":52307}],"status":"original_classroom_note_sample","basis":"provided_book_pdf_and_markdown","followUpExplanation":"An action potential is a brief, regenerated electrical event that travels along an axon without the progressive weakening expected of a simple passive signal.","followUpParagraphIndex":52103,"depth":"comprehensive_masters_with_expanded_explanations","studyDepth":"standard_existing"},{"headingId":"bp14-m1-3-h05","title":"The All-or-None Law","level":2,"parentId":"bp14-m1-3-h04","printedPage":28,"pdfPage":46,"explanation":"The all-or-none law means that crossing threshold triggers an action potential of approximately fixed size and propagation speed for that axon. A stronger initial stimulus does not make the individual spike much taller.","paragraphIndex":20012,"bullets":[{"label":"Coding intensity","explanation":"Stronger input may make spikes occur more often or recruit additional neurons; rate and timing convey differences in stimulus strength.","paragraphIndex":20013},{"label":"Important distinction","explanation":"Subthreshold potentials are graded, while axonal action potentials regenerate. Do not confuse a neuron's firing frequency with the size of one action potential.","paragraphIndex":20014},{"label":"Threshold","explanation":"A below-threshold change does not generate the full spike; reaching threshold initiates one.","paragraphIndex":52308},{"label":"Representing intensity","explanation":"Stronger input can change how frequently a neuron fires and which neurons are recruited, rather than making one neuron's individual spikes proportionally larger.","paragraphIndex":52309}],"status":"original_classroom_note_sample","basis":"provided_book_pdf_and_markdown","followUpExplanation":"The all-or-none law refers to the approximate amplitude of a single action potential once threshold is reached. Understanding the sequence explains why a spike is fast, brief and self-limiting.","paragraphIndex":20015,"bullets":[{"label":"Rising phase","explanation":"Voltage-gated sodium channels open and sodium enters, rapidly depolarizing the membrane. The inward electrical and concentration forces reinforce this movement.","paragraphIndex":20016},{"label":"Recovery","explanation":"Sodium channels inactivate while potassium conductance rises, allowing positive charge to leave and voltage to return toward rest; brief overshoot can follow.","paragraphIndex":20017},{"label":"Rising phase","explanation":"Opening of sodium channels promotes inward sodium movement and rapid depolarization.","paragraphIndex":52310},{"label":"Recovery phase","explanation":"Sodium channels inactivate while potassium permeability increases, driving the membrane back toward its resting voltage. Pumps preserve the ion gradients over time, rather than supplying the immediate spike waveform.","paragraphIndex":52311}],"status":"original_classroom_note_sample","basis":"provided_book_pdf_and_markdown","followUpExplanation":"The spike depends on the changing permeability of the membrane to sodium and potassium. The signal is regenerated rather than carried like a gradually weakening wave.","paragraphIndex":20018,"bullets":[{"label":"Local circuit","explanation":"Current from one active region depolarizes neighboring membrane and triggers its voltage-gated channels.","paragraphIndex":20019},{"label":"Direction","explanation":"Refractory membrane behind the advancing spike normally prevents an immediate second firing there; activity can also back-propagate toward dendrites in relevant contexts.","paragraphIndex":20020},{"label":"Local current","explanation":"A spike depolarizes the adjacent membrane enough to open its voltage-dependent channels.","paragraphIndex":52312},{"label":"Direction","explanation":"The recently active region becomes refractory, helping the wave normally move forward rather than endlessly reactivating the segment behind it.","paragraphIndex":52313}],"status":"original_classroom_note_sample","basis":"provided_book_pdf_and_markdown","followUpExplanation":"Propagation is the repeated regeneration of an action potential in neighboring portions of an axon. This refractory behavior limits firing rate and contributes to reliable direction of impulse flow.","paragraphIndex":20021,"bullets":[{"label":"Absolute period","explanation":"While sodium channels are inactivated, another spike cannot be generated, no matter how strong the usual stimulus.","paragraphIndex":20022},{"label":"Relative period","explanation":"As channels recover and potassium conductance remains elevated, a stronger-than-normal input may be required to reach threshold.","paragraphIndex":20023},{"label":"Absolute refractory period","explanation":"Recently activated sodium channels are inactivated, so another normal spike cannot immediately occur.","paragraphIndex":52314},{"label":"Relative refractory period","explanation":"As the membrane recovers, a stronger-than-usual stimulus may be required. The signal does not literally leap through empty space; local current passes beneath insulated membrane between nodes.","paragraphIndex":52317}],"status":"original_classroom_note_sample","basis":"provided_book_pdf_and_markdown","followUpExplanation":"Myelin is an insulating covering around segments of many axons. It makes conduction faster by concentrating spike regeneration at gaps between insulated segments.","followUpParagraphIndex":52108,"depth":"comprehensive_masters_with_expanded_explanations","studyDepth":"standard_existing"},{"headingId":"bp14-m1-3-h10","title":"Local Neurons","level":1,"parentId":null,"printedPage":33,"pdfPage":51,"explanation":"Some small interneurons communicate through local graded changes rather than conventional long-distance axonal action potentials. This adds a second important mode of neural signaling.","paragraphIndex":20027,"bullets":[{"label":"Graded response","explanation":"A larger input can produce a larger local voltage change, which diminishes as it spreads.","paragraphIndex":20028},{"label":"Circuit function","explanation":"Local neurons often provide inhibition, helping networks filter, shape and coordinate information instead of exciting everything simultaneously.","paragraphIndex":20029},{"label":"Graded potentials","explanation":"Without a conventional axon, some local neurons use variable membrane-voltage changes that do not follow the all-or-none rule.","paragraphIndex":52318},{"label":"Circuit role","explanation":"Such cells can modulate nearby neurons and fine-tune local processing instead of sending messages across long distances.","paragraphIndex":52319}],"status":"original_classroom_note_sample","basis":"provided_book_pdf_and_markdown","followUpExplanation":"Many small local neurons communicate over very short distances and do not rely on the long-axon spike pattern.
